strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: joint co-design of robot morphology and reward/control, where body and behavior are tightly coupled.

Proposes a structured multi-agent LLM debate framework (thesis-antithesis-synthesis) with physics-simulator feedback and pluralistic judges, combining ideas from LLM debate, reward design, and robot co-design.
Separates the training reward from the evaluation score to reduce reward hacking, and uses simulator-in-the-loop evaluation for objective feedback.

Reports a promising preliminary result on Ant locomotion: the D2C-discovered design-reward pair scores 6421.67 versus 3715.42 for default Ant, with qualitatively different reward terms encouraging stability and smoothness.
Includes an honest limitations section acknowledging the single-task evaluation, constrained design edits, computational cost, and prompt sensitivity.
weaknesses: The central claims that D2C outperforms single-agent pipelines and is the 'first multi-agent LLM formulation for robot co-design' are not empirically supported. The only comparison is against the default Ant baseline; there is no comparison to single-agent LLM baselines, Eureka-style reward design, or existing LLM co-design methods such as RoboMoRe, Text2Robot, or VLMgineer.

There is a serious inconsistency between Figure 2 and Table I: Figure 2 shows a Round 5 synthesis score near 36,000 on the y-axis ('Distance from Origin'), while Table I reports the best D2C score as 6421.67 and baseline as 3715.42. The text claims both are forward-distance score S. This undermines confidence in the main quantitative evidence.

Evaluation is limited to a single task and environment (Brax Ant locomotion), with no independent runs over the debate process or LLM stochasticity. The reported confidence intervals are only across multiple reward candidates within one debate run, not across seeds or repeated debates, so robustness is not established.

The final design-reward pair is selected from the archive using the same score S that drives optimization, with no held-out evaluation. This risks overfitting to simulation noise and candidate-selection variance, especially given the very large error bars in later rounds.

The algorithm and text mismatch: the control agent generates reward r_k from the thesis morphology m_k^{th}, but Algorithm 1 then trains both thesis and synthesis designs with that same r_k. The text states the reward is tailored to the new design, but the synthesis design is not given a reward conditioned on itself. This weakens the claimed dialectical coupling.

No ablations isolate the contributions of the debate protocol, pluralistic judges, hall-of-fame archive, multiple reward candidates, or control agent. The paper also claims emergent diversity and specialized morphologies without quantifying diversity or analyzing novelty.

Reproducibility is poor: no code, prompts, reward templates, LLM/judge configurations, hyperparameters (K, PPO training steps, seeds, number of candidates), compute details, or implementation specifics are provided. The LLM is described only as 'GPT-5,' with no version or API details.

Presentation is incomplete for a main-track paper: key methodological details are missing (exposed design parameters, edit bounds, judge prompts, feedback integration), and the figure/table inconsistency makes the main results difficult to interpret.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely meaningful problem: joint co-design of morphology and reward, which is well-motivated by the tight body-behavior coupling discussed in the introduction.

Grounding the "judges" in physics-simulation metrics rather than learned arbiters of argument persuasiveness is a sensible design choice that avoids the known pitfalls of LLM-judged debates, and the explicit separation of the training reward from a shared evaluation score S is a good principle for mitigating reward hacking.
The related-work section is reasonably thorough and positions the work against RoboMorph, LASER, RoboMoRe, and Eureka.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging the single-task evaluation, constrained parametric edits, computational scaling, and prompt sensitivity.
weaknesses: No baselines or ablations are reported. The central claim in Fig. 1 that multi-agent debate finds designs "single-agent methods would miss" is never tested; there is no single-agent comparison, no comparison against RoboMorph/LASER/RoboMoRe/Eureka, and no ablation of any debate component (thesis, antithesis, synthesis, pluralistic judges). The core contribution is therefore asserted, not demonstrated.

The experimental scope is far too thin to support the paper's general claims. Results come from a single task (Brax Ant) over only 5 debate rounds, and the paper itself calls these "preliminary results" in the introduction. This is insufficient for the sweeping conclusions about a "new paradigm" for robot design.

The evidence is statistically unconvincing. Figure 2 shows enormous 95% CIs (the round-5 synthesis interval spans roughly an order of magnitude), and the intervals are computed over only ~4 reward candidates per design rather than over independent runs/seeds. The claim that "synthesis consistently outperforms thesis" and the headline 73% improvement are not supported by a variance-controlled comparison; the reported advantage could easily be noise.

The "emergent diversity" claim (a key selling point in Fig. 1 and the abstract) is not quantified at all. There is no diversity metric, only a qualitative statement and an illustrative figure, so the claim that specialized morphologies emerge without an explicit diversity objective is unsubstantiated.

Algorithm 1 is internally inconsistent: the synthesis step (line 5) revises the design using FEEDBACK(m_k^th, r_k) before the thesis is ever trained/evaluated (lines 6-9), so the source of that feedback is undefined. This undermines the credibility of the described debate protocol.

The role of the "pluralistic judges" is unclear. They produce textual feedback, but the final selection is by the scalar score S, so the paper never shows that the multi-judge mechanism changes outcomes; it may be decorative relative to a simple score-based search.

Reproducibility is weak: the agents use a proprietary model (GPT-5), prompt templates are not provided, the reward template and PPO training budget are unspecified, and no code/data release is mentioned, making independent verification difficult.

Novelty is incremental and not isolated. RoboMoRe already alternates LLM morphology edits with reward hints, and Eureka already generates reward code; the paper's distinguishing element (structured debate + pluralistic judges) is not experimentally separated from these prior methods.

Minor presentation issues, e.g., Figure 2 labels the y-axis "Distance from Origin" while the text describes "forward distance," and the strong framing ("first multi-agent LLM formulation for robot co-design," "powerful, scalable approach") overstates what a single 5-round Ant experiment can support.

strengths: The core framing—applying structured multi-agent LLM debate (thesis–antithesis–synthesis) to joint morphology-reward co-design with a physics simulator as the arbiter—is a genuinely fresh and conceptually appealing angle relative to single-agent LLM design pipelines.
The design choice to separate the training reward from the evaluation score S (to avoid specification gaming) is sensible and well-justified in Section II-A.

The pluralistic-judge panel and hall-of-fame archive are reasonable mechanisms for balancing multiple objectives and reusing good candidates, and the related-work discussion situates the work clearly among RoboMorph, LASER, Eureka, and RoboMoRe.
The paper is generally readable and the algorithm/pipeline (Algorithm 1, Fig. 1) is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central claim—that debate 'uncovers novel, high-performing morphologies beyond what single-agent pipelines achieve'—is never tested. The only comparison is against the default Ant robot; there is no single-agent baseline, no debate-vs-no-debate ablation, and no ablation of the pluralistic judges or the archive. The paper's headline contribution is therefore unsupported by the experiments.

Evaluation is extremely thin: a single task (Brax Ant locomotion), which the authors themselves describe as 'preliminary results' in the Introduction. No diversity metric is reported even though 'emergent diversity over debate rounds' is claimed in Fig. 1C.

There is a serious numerical inconsistency: Figure 2 shows synthesis scores reaching ~35,000 (with 95% CIs up to ~60,000) by Round 5, yet Table I reports the best design-reward pair at only 6421.67. The metric is also ambiguous—the figure labels the axis 'Distance from Origin' while the text defines S as forward distance. This undermines confidence in the reported results and in reproducibility.

Statistical treatment is weak: the 95% CIs are computed over reward candidates for a single design, not over independent seeds/runs of the method. The reported 73% improvement appears driven almost entirely by one noisy Round-5 point with enormous variance, and no significance testing or multi-seed replication is provided.

The thesis-vs-synthesis comparison is confounded: both morphologies are evaluated under the same reward r_k, and synthesis is simply a revision of thesis, so this does not isolate the benefit of the debate mechanism itself.

Reproducibility is inadequate: prompts, LLM hyperparameters, training budget (number of PPO steps), number of seeds, and code are not provided, and the system relies on a proprietary closed model (GPT-5), making independent replication difficult.
The claimed distinction from RoboMoRe (also an LLM morphology+reward co-design method) as 'principled' versus 'ad-hoc alternating heuristics' is asserted rather than demonstrated empirically.

The computational cost/scalability of the approach (up to eight trainings per round, K rounds) is acknowledged as a limitation but never quantified, and the sensitivity to prompt templates is not examined.

strengths: Introduces a novel integration of multi-agent debate, role-separated design/control agents, pluralistic LLM judges, and simulator-grounded selection for joint morphology-reward co-design, with a clear algorithm and framework description.

Conducts extensive experiments on five MuJoCo locomotion tasks with multiple baselines and ablations (zero-shot, single-agent, thesis-only, judges, LLM backbone), and provides detailed appendices including prompts, hyperparameters, compute budget, and example reward functions, supporting some reproducibility.

Shows that iterative debate improves over compute-matched zero-shot generation and that D2C-generated rewards transfer to default morphologies in 4/5 tasks, suggesting the learned shaping captures some generalizable locomotion principles.
Includes an honest limitations section acknowledging compute cost, simulation-only evaluation, and the parametric design space, and provides an appropriate impact statement.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metric S (cumulative distance from origin) is non-standard and only moderately correlated with standard MuJoCo returns (mean Spearman ρ=0.61; Swimmer Pearson r=-0.01). It can be gamed by backward, sideways, or oscillatory motion and ignores survival, energy, and stability, so headline gains (e.g., 3.2× on Ant, ~9× on Swimmer) may not reflect true task performance. The poor top-10 overlap with standard returns (mean 1.0/10) and the uncorrelated Swimmer metric further undermine the main claims.

Baselines are not fully fair: Bayesian optimization optimizes morphology only under a fixed default reward and is therefore not a true co-design baseline, while RoboMoRe is reimplemented inside the authors' Brax stack, which may underperform the original method. Zero scores on some tasks may reflect these implementation and metric choices rather than fundamental method limitations.

Statistical power is low: only 3 search seeds are used, and final evaluation retrains the same best pair 5 times, so search variance and selection bias are not properly quantified. Several comparisons are not significant after FDR correction (e.g., Ant vs. BO, HalfCheetah vs. Eureka), and the paper relies heavily on effect sizes rather than robust significance testing.

The pluralistic-judges ablation is mixed: judges improve hypervolume on some tasks but not HalfCheetah, where the no-judges condition is better, and the authors acknowledge that the stability judge can dilute feedback in Swimmer/HalfCheetah. The control-agent critique is not isolated in any ablation, so the claim that critiques prevent unstable designs is not directly tested.

Reproducibility is compromised by reliance on a proprietary, future-dated model GPT-5.2 (gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) without details on temperature, sampling seeds, or long-term API availability. Citation years are inconsistent (e.g., Cheney et al. 2018 cited as 2023; Ng et al. 1999 cited as 2023), indicating insufficient care in preparation.

The reward-similarity analysis appears too coarse: Eureka and Default/BO rewards show cosine similarity 1.00, raising doubts about whether the AST feature vectors can meaningfully distinguish reward structures, which weakens the claim that D2C generates structurally distinct rewards.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel combination of multi-agent LLM debate with robot morphology-reward co-design, grounded in physics simulation, which is a creative extension of existing ideas.
The presentation is clear and well-organized, with helpful figures (e.g., the framework overview and debate dynamics) and a detailed appendix covering prompts and hyperparameters.
The limitations section is honest about compute costs, simulator dependence, and the small number of seeds, which is commendable.
The framework is modular and could be extended to other design spaces or tasks, and the idea of using pluralistic judges for multi-objective feedback is interesting.
weaknesses: Statistical evidence is weak: only 3 search seeds are used, and many key comparisons are not statistically significant (e.g., Ant vs. Bayesian Optimization p=0.0655). Effect sizes with n=3 are unreliable and cannot support strong claims of outperformance.

Key ablations (zero-shot generation, role separation, pluralistic judges) lack rigorous statistical reporting. Results are often shown only as learning curves without tables, p-values, or effect sizes, making it difficult to assess whether the improvements are meaningful.

Baselines are potentially unfair: Bayesian Optimization optimizes morphology only and is structurally disadvantaged in a joint co-design comparison. RoboMoRe, when reimplemented, achieves zero scores on some tasks, raising questions about evaluation fidelity and whether the comparison is apples-to-apples.

The evaluation metric S (cumulative distance) correlates only moderately with standard returns (Spearman ρ=0.61 overall, and ρ=0.39 for Swimmer), which may bias selection and compromise the validity of the performance comparisons.

The transfer claim (rewards transfer to default morphologies in 4/5 tasks) is based on modest, inconsistent gains without statistical tests. For example, in Hopper the morphology-only condition performs worse than default, and Swimmer shows little room for reward shaping.
The zero-shot baseline is not fully described—it is unclear whether it is a strong baseline or a strawman, and no per-environment statistics are provided to support the claimed 18–35% gains.
Reproducibility is limited: the proprietary LLM (GPT-5.2) has no public version details, and code is not yet released, making exact replication difficult.

The paper overclaims in the abstract and introduction, stating that D2C 'outperforms prior LLM-based methods and black-box optimization,' while the evidence is inconclusive due to small sample sizes and weak statistical support.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: joint morphology-reward co-design for robot locomotion, where body and control objective are tightly coupled.
Introduces a well-motivated multi-agent LLM framework that combines role-separated debate, critique-then-synthesis refinement, pluralistic judge feedback, and simulator-grounded selection.
The main empirical claim that iterative debate improves over single-pass generation is supported by comparisons against zero-shot, single-agent, and thesis-only ablations across five MuJoCo tasks.
Reports strong performance improvements over prior LLM-based and black-box baselines, including up to ~3.2x on Ant and ~9x on Swimmer, with statistical tests and effect sizes.
The transfer experiment showing D2C-generated rewards improve default morphologies in 4/5 tasks is a useful indication of generalizable reward shaping rather than purely morphology-specific hacking.

The separation between the reward used for policy training and the standardized evaluation score S is a sound design choice for reducing specification gaming and making cross-method comparisons fairer.
Provides substantial reproducibility details: full prompts, RL hyperparameters, compute budgets, example reward expressions, and a promise to release code and configurations.
Includes an honest limitations section discussing compute cost, simulator dependence, sim-to-real gaps, design-space restrictions, and small-scale evaluation.
weaknesses: The contribution of the pluralistic judges is not convincingly supported for the main objective. Figure 6 shows that on HalfCheetah (2D) the no-judges condition substantially outperforms pluralistic judges, and the paper only reports hypervolume rather than final task score S with and without judges. The claim that judges improve multi-objective coverage is therefore qualified and partially contradicted.

There are reporting inconsistencies that reduce confidence in the experimental claims. The text states Eureka uses 5 search seeds/runs versus D2C's 3, but Table 7 reports only 3 seeds for Eureka. The critique-action correlation analysis states there are 60 design changes, yet Table 8 reports observed co-occurrence counts summing to well over 300, making the chi-squared analysis internally inconsistent as presented.

The evaluation metric S (cumulative distance from origin) is non-standard and only moderately correlated with standard episode returns (mean Spearman rho = 0.61; Swimmer Pearson r = -0.01). The top-10 overlap between S-ranked and return-ranked candidates is low (mean 1/10), so it is unclear how well the reported gains translate to standard MuJoCo locomotion performance.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair in places. BO and RoboMoRe achieve zero scores on some tasks, and RoboMoRe is adapted into the authors' Brax stack rather than evaluated in its native setting. The paper also does not fully clarify whether PPO/SAC selection was tuned per morphology for D2C, which could advantage D2C over baselines.

Statistical power is limited: main comparisons use only n = 3 search seeds, some comparisons have zero variance (making t-tests undefined), and several claims rest on effect sizes and visual trends rather than robust significance testing.

The 'compute-matched' zero-shot ablation appears matched only in RL candidate budget, not in LLM token/compute budget; D2C uses additional debate and judge calls, so the comparison is not fully compute-matched end-to-end.
Reliance on a proprietary LLM backbone (GPT-5.2, gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) limits exact reproducibility and independent verification, even with prompts and hyperparameters provided.

The novelty is largely an integration of existing ideas (LLM reward design, LLM morphology search, multi-agent debate, pluralistic judges). The 'first' claims are somewhat overclaimed, as RoboMoRe also jointly optimizes morphology and reward with an LLM, albeit without multi-agent debate.

Presentation quality is weakened by numerous citation-year mismatches (e.g., Chan et al. 2016 vs. 2023; Du et al. 2021 vs. 2023; Mania et al. 2023 vs. 2018; Ng et al. 2023 vs. 1999; Todorov et al. 2024 vs. 2012) and some table/text inconsistencies that should be corrected.

The framework is evaluated only in simulation on five parametric MuJoCo locomotion tasks with fixed topology; no real-robot validation is provided, and the sim-to-real gap remains a significant limitation for the claimed robot co-design impact.
